children: Banks and financial services firms accounted for 60% of all long-term corporate bond issuance in India since January 2025, while auto, textile, and IT firms raised about 1% combined, according to data from PRIME Database.

Financial services and investment firms raised ₹6.53 lakh crore through bonds maturing in more than a year between January 2025 and September 2026, more than any other industry. Banks and term-lending institutions raised a further ₹5.22 lakh crore.

“Lagging deposit growth is possibly prompting banks to opt for market borrowings, as credit growth continues to outpace deposit growth,” said Dnyanada Vaidya, Equity Research Analyst at Axis Securities.
The divergence in debt issuance reflects how differently these sectors use capital. Banks and non-bank lenders borrow continuously to fund their own lending books.

The skew is largely structural, said Venkatakrishnan Srinivasan, founder and managing partner at Rockfort Fincap LLP. Banks, NBFCs and housing finance companies have a continuous requirement to raise debt to fund their loan books, he said.

NBFCs with floating-rate loan assets, debt-capital markets remain an important funding source given elevated swap rates, keeping the financial services segment's share of issuers high, according to Basant Bafna, Head- Fixed Income, Mirae Asset Mutual Fund.

The investor side reinforces the pattern, Srinivasan said, with AAA- and AA-rated borrowers accounting for more than 80% of bond issuance, a bar that large, established financial institutions clear more easily than most industrial borrowers.

Large IT and automobile companies are relatively cash-generative and therefore do not have the same recurring requirement for long-term debt. Their borrowing tends to be linked instead to working capital, capex, refinancing or acquisitions.
This pattern has only recently begun to shift, with private sector capex and related borrowing starting to pick up.
The top five industries- financial services, banking, housing, power, and housing finance- accounted for more than 81% of the ₹19.41 lakh crore raised across all sectors.
For banks, bonds could be viewed as a complementary source of longer-tenor funding and a means of diversifying their liability profile, said Vaidya.

Manufacturing sectors raised a fraction of what financial firms did. Passenger vehicle makers raised ₹4,030 crore over the period, textile companies ₹2,407 crore, and IT software firms, among India's largest exporters, just ₹13,936 crore, or 0.72% of the total.
"The size of an industry does not automatically translate into a large share of bond issuance," Srinivasan said.
Bajaj Housing Finance alone raised more than ₹6,500 crore through repeat bond sales between June and September 2026, more than textile companies raised since January last year.

Under SEBI's large corporate framework, eligible large corporations are required to raise at least 25% of incremental borrowings through debt securities, a rule designed to widen the issuer base beyond financial institutions.

title: Banks, financial firms drive 60% of India bond sales
